title: Other Gardens Worth Visiting
author: Andrew Cantarutti
summary: The closing installment of Andrew Cantarutti's six-part series on attention as curriculum is an annotated guide to books and organizations that take attention seriously, which he calls the other gardens. The reading list is organized into three groups: philosophical accounts of what attention is for (Crawford, Weil, Murdoch), accounts of how attention is cultivated (Odell, Kreiner, Jha, Mark), and critiques of how attention is captured by technology and markets (Carr, Han, Wu, Williams, Barba-Kay). Each entry carries a short evaluative gloss, including a caution that Jha and Mark are useful for their science but accept the instrumental view of attention as a resource to be extracted. The second half surveys advocacy groups in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and Australia working on phone-free schools, delayed smartphone adoption and humane technology. Cantarutti frames the walled garden image as protection of the conditions learning needs rather than exclusion of the world, and closes by inviting schools to join the list and to teach attention deliberately.
points: The reading list moves from philosophy of attention to its cultivation and then to its capture by technology, giving the series a canon.
Simone Weil's essay on school studies is presented as the series' touchstone, arguing education exists to train the faculty of attention.
Cantarutti warns that popular attention science books by Jha and Mark treat attention as a resource for productivity rather than a good in itself.
The organizations section maps a transnational phone-free and screen-limiting movement across four countries with concrete toolkits for schools and parents.
quotes: The Walled Garden metaphor is deliberate; a garden doesn’t have walls to exclude the world, but to protect the conditions we know it needs to thrive. In our schools, attention is a precondition for learning.
Crawford makes the case for attention as a shared resource. Like clean air or water, our collective ability to focus is a finite resource.
Aimed clearly, attention is distinct from sheer willpower; it is patient, quiet, and receptive — things we could all use more of today.

Freedom, she argues, is only possible when we see the world clearly. Therefore, if freedom requires an increasing knowledge of reality, the proper orientation of our attention is its precondition. If we can’t attend, we can’t be free.

Both Jha’s and Mark’s books prove valuable for their presentation of neuroscientific research and longitudinal data, but both fall into the trap of accepting the modern instrumentalization of our attention as a resource to be extracted and expended for economic means and productivity optimization.
He makes the distinction between “deep attention” — slow, immersive contemplation — and today’s more common “hyperattention” — a scattered state characterized by multitasking and digital media.
We need schools that create the conditions for healthy attention to flourish, and a curriculum that teaches attention to our students deliberately.
